title: A rush of memories
text:
When reading “A tale of California’s gold rush, rich in nuggets,” a review of Nathaniel Philbrick’s new book, “The Rush” (Nov. 16 Monitor Weekly), I was reminded of Richard Henry Dana Jr.’s memoir, “Two Years Before the Mast,” which I had recently read. Dana’s book relates his voyage in the mid-1830s around Cape Horn from Boston to the California coast, where his ship traded East Coast merchandise for locally produced cattle hides. The California he describes is a largely forested rural backwater whose primary economic activity is small-scale farming.
When Dana revisits California 25 years later, as related in the book’s last chapter, he finds that the local cattle industry has been displaced by the rise of cattle ranching for meat in the Great Plains. These ranches were large-scale operations, often covering tens of thousands of acres of natural grassland. The cattle were herded to railroad depots, from which they were shipped live to slaughterhouses in the East. The ranchers had the advantages of economy of scale, and cheaper and faster transport. This circumstance left most of Southern California, including the port city of San Diego, if anything more economically depressed than on his first visit. San Francisco and its surroundings, on the other hand, were booming. Dana does not explain this transformation, which is why I’m eager to read Mr. Philbrick’s book, which hopefully will fill in the 25-year gap in Dana’s book. “Mayflower,” Mr. Philbrick’s book on the Pilgrims, is excellent.
Eric Klieber
Cleveland Heights, Ohio
